code: p_control <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.25, 0.20, 0.12, 0.08, 0.05) p_program <- rev(p_control)  rating_mean <- function(p) sum(1:7 * p) rating_var <- function(p) sum((1:7 - rating_mean(p))^2 * p) true_delta <- (rating_mean(p_program) - rating_mean(p_control)) /   sqrt((rating_var(p_program) + rating_var(p_control)) / 2) true_delta #> [1] 0.6487847  one_study <- function(width = 0.80, batch = 10) {   m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = width)   program <- sample(7, m, replace = TRUE, prob = p_program)   control <- sample(7, m, replace = TRUE, prob = p_control)   repeat {     out <- seq_aipe_smd(program, control, width = width)     if (attr(out, "is_satisfied")) break     program <- c(program, sample(7, batch, replace = TRUE, prob = p_program))     control <- c(control, sample(7, batch, replace = TRUE, prob = p_control))   }   summary(out) }  set.seed(113) studies <- do.call(rbind, replicate(100, one_study(), simplify = FALSE)) covered <- with(studies, lower_limit <= true_delta & true_delta <= upper_limit) c(mean_n = mean(studies$current_n), coverage = mean(covered)) #>   mean_n coverage  #>    61.60     0.97 one_mean_study <- function(d = 0.5, mu = 10, sigma = 2) {   x <- rnorm(seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = d), mean = mu, sd = sigma)   repeat {     out <- seq_fwd_norm_mean(x, d = d)     if (attr(out, "is_satisfied")) break     x <- c(x, rnorm(1, mean = mu, sd = sigma))   }   summary(out) }  set.seed(113) mean_studies <- do.call(rbind, replicate(100, one_mean_study(),                                          simplify = FALSE)) mean_covered <- with(mean_studies, lower_limit <= 10 & 10 <= upper_limit) c(mean_n = mean(mean_studies$current_n), coverage = mean(mean_covered)) #>   mean_n coverage  #>    59.25     0.89

code: # Is a cheaper online training format (group 1) no worse, by more than # 3 points, than the average of two established formats? set.seed(113) weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5) costs <- c(10, 38, 15) true_means <- c(50, 50, 50) scores <- lapply(true_means, function(m) rnorm(10, mean = m, sd = 6)) repeat {   out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = 3000)   g <- seq_budget_next(out)   if (is.na(g)) break   scores[[g]] <- c(scores[[g]], rnorm(1, mean = true_means[g], sd = 6)) } out #> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast) #>  #>   Current n       : 192 #>   Criterion n     : 194 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>  #>   lower_limit       : -0.8960654 #>   contrast          : 0.8640861 #>   upper_limit       : 2.624238 #>   variance          : 0.8064992 #>   current_total_n   : 192 #>   current_total_cost: 2995 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE (sampling has ended: the budget is exhausted) #>  #>   Note: Sampling has ended because the budget cannot pay for another #>         observation: 5 of 3000 is left, and one more observation from a #>         group still below its criterion (groups 1 and 3) costs at least #>         10.  # Noninferiority with a margin of 3 points, at one-sided level 0.05. decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(out, margin = 3) #> [1] TRUE  # The same test, as the special case margin = -abs(3) of superiority. decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = -abs(3)) #> [1] TRUE  # Is the online format better than the average of the other two at all, # or worse than it? decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = 0) #> [1] FALSE decide_seq_budget_inferiority(out, margin = 0) #> [1] FALSE  # Equivalence within 3 points either way: two one-sided tests at 0.05, # and then at a much stricter level. decide_seq_budget_equivalence(out, margin_lower = -3, margin_upper = 3) #> [1] TRUE decide_seq_budget_equivalence(out, margin_lower = -3, margin_upper = 3,                               alpha_level = 0.005) #> [1] FALSE

code: # Annual salaries (in thousands of dollars) of ten employees of a firm: # two employees chosen at random differ by this much on average. salary <- c(28, 31, 35, 38, 42, 47, 55, 64, 90, 170) gini_mean_diff(salary) #> [1] 42.04444  # The Gini index is the mean difference over twice the mean. gini_mean_diff(salary) / (2 * mean(salary)) #> [1] 0.3503704 gini_index(salary) #> [1] 0.3503704

code: set.seed(113) # Satisfaction (1 to 7 scale) and weekly hours of product use for 150 # customers, in the order surveyed. How does the interval for their # correlation narrow toward a full width of 0.30? use <- rnorm(150, mean = 10, sd = 3) satisfaction <- 4 + 0.15 * (use - 10) + rnorm(150, sd = 0.8) path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_r, list(use, satisfaction), width = 0.30) plot(path)   # One panel, with the vertical axis and its label chosen by the user. plot(path, which = "estimate", ylim = c(0, 1.2), las = 1,      ylab = expression(hat(rho)))

The goal is a 95% confidence interval for the # population squared multiple correlation no wider than 0.25. set.seed(113) survey <- function(n) {   predictors <- cbind(autonomy = rnorm(n), support = rnorm(n),                       workload = rnorm(n))   satisfaction <- drop(predictors %*% c(0.45, 0.40, -0.30)) + rnorm(n)   list(x = predictors, y = satisfaction) } m <- seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width = 0.25, p = 3) employees <- survey(m) out <- seq_aipe_R2(employees$x, employees$y, width = 0.25) # Not met, with a note: 32 observations are few for three predictors. out #> Sequential check (squared multiple correlation, Wald interval) #>  #>   Current n       : 32 #>   Criterion n     : 104 #>   Target width    : 0.25 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : 0.42985 #>   R2                : 0.6324142 #>   upper_limit       : 0.8349784 #>   xi_squared        : 0.3418055 #>   criterion_n       : 104 #>   current_n         : 32 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE #>  #>   Note: With 32 observations and 3 predictors the sample is small #>         relative to the number of predictors (fewer than 60 #>         observations, 20 per predictor). The sample squared multiple #>         correlation then overestimates the population value, and in #>         simulations the interval of this procedure contained the #>         population value less often than the confidence level, far less #>         often the smaller the sample. This note does not change the #>         stopping rule. See 'Small Samples Relative to the Number of #>         Predictors' in the help of seq_aipe_R2().  # Survey ten more employees at a time until the stopping rule is met. while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   more <- survey(10)   employees <- list(x = rbind(employees$x, more$x),                     y = c(employees$y, more$y))   out <- seq_aipe_R2(employees$x, employees$y, width = 0.25) } out #> Sequential check (squared multiple correlation, Wald interval) #>  #>   Current n       : 152 #>   Criterion n     : 149 #>   Target width    : 0.25 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : 0.2709712 #>   R2                : 0.3920038 #>   upper_limit       : 0.5130364 #>   xi_squared        : 0.5796315 #>   criterion_n       : 149 #>   current_n         : 152 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE  # The same data one employee at a time, as a path. seq_path() cannot work # out the pilot sample size for this procedure (it depends on the number # of predictors), so the start is supplied. path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_R2, employees, width = 0.25,                  start = seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width = 0.25, p = 3)) attr(path, "stop_n") #> [1] 149 # The check at the stopping point. Its notes, if it has any, are shown # here and not when the path itself is printed. attr(path, "final_check") #> Sequential check (squared multiple correlation, Wald interval) #>  #>   Current n       : 149 #>   Criterion n     : 149 #>   Target width    : 0.25 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : 0.2688058 #>   R2                : 0.3910916 #>   upper_limit       : 0.5133775 #>   xi_squared        : 0.5800192 #>   criterion_n       : 149 #>   current_n         : 149 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

code: # Does a new onboarding program change first year performance ratings # (standardized) relative to the average of two existing programs? The # aim is a 95% confidence interval for that contrast no wider than 0.80. set.seed(113) program_means <- c(new = 0.5, existing_a = 0, existing_b = 0) weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5) m <- seq_aipe_c_pilot(width = 0.80) ratings <- lapply(program_means, function(mu) rnorm(m, mean = mu)) out <- seq_aipe_c(ratings, weights, width = 0.80) out #> Sequential check (contrast) #>  #>   Current n       : 5 #>   Criterion n     : 42 #>   Target width    : 0.8 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : -0.3410512 #>   contrast          : 0.7461581 #>   upper_limit       : 1.833367 #>   xi_squared        : 1.538509 #>   criterion_n       : 42 #>   current_n         : 5 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # The rule is not met at the pilot. code: # How strongly are citizenship behavior at work and neuroticism related? # The aim is a 95% confidence interval for the correlation that is no # wider than 0.30. set.seed(113) new_pairs <- function(k, rho = -0.3) {   citizenship <- rnorm(k)   cbind(citizenship, rho * citizenship + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(k)) } scores <- new_pairs(seq_aipe_r_pilot(width = 0.30)) out <- seq_aipe_r(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], width = 0.30) out #> Sequential check (Pearson correlation) #>  #>   Current n       : 14 #>   Criterion n     : 102 #>   Target width    : 0.3 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : -0.7589524 #>   r                 : -0.3790672 #>   upper_limit       : 0.0008179968 #>   xi_squared        : 0.5259405 #>   criterion_n       : 102 #>   current_n         : 14 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # The rule is not met at the pilot. Add one employee at a time and check # again, until it is. while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   scores <- rbind(scores, new_pairs(1))   out <- seq_aipe_r(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], width = 0.30) } out #> Sequential check (Pearson correlation) #>  #>   Current n       : 125 #>   Criterion n     : 124 #>   Target width    : 0.3 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : -0.3967731 #>   r                 : -0.2487647 #>   upper_limit       : -0.1007562 #>   xi_squared        : 0.7128316 #>   criterion_n       : 124 #>   current_n         : 125 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE  # Kendall's tau from the same data and target seq_aipe_r(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], width = 0.30, method = "kendall") #> Sequential check (Kendall correlation) #>  #>   Current n       : 125 #>   Criterion n     : 70 #>   Target width    : 0.3 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : -0.2759581 #>   r                 : -0.1654194 #>   upper_limit       : -0.05488058 #>   xi_squared        : 0.397597 #>   criterion_n       : 70 #>   current_n         : 125 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

code: # How much does job satisfaction change per standard deviation of # perceived autonomy (both standardized)? The aim is a 95% confidence # interval for the slope that is no wider than 0.40. set.seed(113) m <- seq_aipe_reg_coef_pilot(width = 0.40, m_0 = 20) autonomy <- rnorm(m) satisfaction <- 0.5 * autonomy + rnorm(m, sd = sqrt(0.75)) out <- seq_aipe_reg_coef(autonomy, satisfaction, width = 0.40) out #> Sequential check (simple linear regression slope) #>  #>   Current n       : 20 #>   Criterion n     : 103 #>   Target width    : 0.4 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : -0.2773156 #>   reg_coef          : 0.1640938 #>   upper_limit       : 0.6055032 #>   xi_squared        : 1.014418 #>   criterion_n       : 103 #>   current_n         : 20 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # The rule is not met at the pilot. Add one employee at a time and check # again, until it is. while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   new_autonomy <- rnorm(1)   autonomy <- c(autonomy, new_autonomy)   satisfaction <- c(satisfaction,                     0.5 * new_autonomy + rnorm(1, sd = sqrt(0.75)))   out <- seq_aipe_reg_coef(autonomy, satisfaction, width = 0.40) } out #> Sequential check (simple linear regression slope) #>  #>   Current n       : 89 #>   Criterion n     : 89 #>   Target width    : 0.4 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : 0.1485017 #>   reg_coef          : 0.347154 #>   upper_limit       : 0.5458064 #>   xi_squared        : 0.9142845 #>   criterion_n       : 89 #>   current_n         : 89 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

code: # By how many standard deviations does a reading score change from fall # to spring? The data are the students' change scores, and the aim is a # 95% confidence interval for the standardized mean change that is no # wider than 0.50. set.seed(113) m <- seq_aipe_sm_pilot(width = 0.50) change <- rnorm(m, mean = 4, sd = 10) out <- seq_aipe_sm(change, width = 0.50) out #> Sequential check (standardized mean) #>  #>   Current n       : 8 #>   Criterion n     : 69 #>   Target width    : 0.5 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : -0.6051389 #>   sm                : 0.0815806 #>   upper_limit       : 0.7683001 #>   xi_squared        : 0.9820929 #>   criterion_n       : 69 #>   current_n         : 8 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # The rule is not met at the pilot. Add one student at a time and check # again, until it is. while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   change <- c(change, rnorm(1, mean = 4, sd = 10))   out <- seq_aipe_sm(change, width = 0.50) } out #> Sequential check (standardized mean) #>  #>   Current n       : 75 #>   Criterion n     : 75 #>   Target width    : 0.5 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : 0.200412 #>   sm                : 0.4477031 #>   upper_limit       : 0.6949941 #>   xi_squared        : 1.193938 #>   criterion_n       : 75 #>   current_n         : 75 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

code: # Does a training program raise employee engagement (rated 1 to 7)? The # aim is a 95% confidence interval for the standardized mean difference # that is no wider than 0.60. set.seed(113) m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = 0.60) trained <- rnorm(m, mean = 4.9, sd = 1) control <- rnorm(m, mean = 4.5, sd = 1) out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60) out #> Sequential check (standardized mean difference) #>  #>   Current n       : 7 #>   Criterion n     : 91 #>   Target width    : 0.6 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : -1.143786 #>   smd               : -0.1011596 #>   upper_limit       : 0.9414664 #>   xi_squared        : 1.980884 #>   criterion_n       : 91 #>   current_n         : 7 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # The rule is not met at the pilot. Add one employee to each group and # check again, until it is. while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   trained <- c(trained, rnorm(1, mean = 4.9, sd = 1))   control <- c(control, rnorm(1, mean = 4.5, sd = 1))   out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60) } out #> Sequential check (standardized mean difference) #>  #>   Current n       : 85 #>   Criterion n     : 85 #>   Target width    : 0.6 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis #>  #>   lower_limit       : 0.05840176 #>   smd               : 0.3564726 #>   upper_limit       : 0.6545434 #>   xi_squared        : 1.965901 #>   criterion_n       : 85 #>   current_n         : 85 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

Incomes are right # skewed; simulated here from a lognormal distribution. set.seed(113) m <- seq_blci_dfr_median_pilot(d = 5, conf_level = 0.95) income <- rlnorm(m, meanlog = log(60), sdlog = 0.5) out <- seq_blci_dfr_median(income, d = 5, conf_level = 0.95) out #> Sequential check (bounded length confidence interval (distribution free)) #>  #>   Current n       : 10 #>   Criterion n     : NA #>   Target width    : 10 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>  #>   lower_limit       : 31.4192 #>   median            : 51.19733 #>   upper_limit       : 87.24341 #>   interval_length   : 55.82421 #>   current_n         : 10 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # Add one household at a time until the stopping rule is met. The note # printed with the result is a reminder that a completed sequential # procedure covers the median somewhat less often than the stated 95% # (see Details). while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   income <- c(income, rlnorm(1, meanlog = log(60), sdlog = 0.5))   out <- seq_blci_dfr_median(income, d = 5, conf_level = 0.95) } out #> Sequential check (bounded length confidence interval (distribution free)) #>  #>   Current n       : 199 #>   Criterion n     : NA #>   Target width    : 10 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>  #>   lower_limit       : 56.09514 #>   median            : 60.46713 #>   upper_limit       : 65.82721 #>   interval_length   : 9.732074 #>   current_n         : 199 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE #>  #>   Note: The confidence level holds for a sample size fixed in advance. #>         A sequential procedure that stops at this check covers the #>         median less often than stated: in simulation, about 0.84 to #>         0.88 for a nominal 0.90, 0.92 to 0.94 for 0.95, and 0.98 to #>         0.99 for 0.99. code: # Scores after a new training format (group 1) and two existing formats. # An observation costs 38, 15, and 10, and the budget is 1,500. set.seed(113) weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5) costs <- c(38, 15, 10) scores <- list(   rnorm(10, mean = 52, sd = 9),   rnorm(10, mean = 50, sd = 6),   rnorm(10, mean = 50, sd = 6) ) out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = 1500) out #> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast) #>  #>   Current n       : 30 #>   Criterion n     : 65 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>  #>   lower_limit       : -9.311685 #>   contrast          : -3.364913 #>   upper_limit       : 2.581859 #>   variance          : 9.205903 #>   current_total_n   : 30 #>   current_total_cost: 630 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE attr(out, "criterion_per_group") #> [1] 29 14 22 attr(out, "remaining_budget") #> [1] 870  # Add one observation at a time, to the group seq_budget_next() names, # until it has none to name. The cost never passes the budget. true_means <- c(52, 50, 50) true_sds <- c(9, 6, 6) repeat {   out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = 1500)   g <- seq_budget_next(out)   if (is.na(g)) break   scores[[g]] <- c(scores[[g]], rnorm(1, true_means[g], true_sds[g])) } out #> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast) #>  #>   Current n       : 65 #>   Criterion n     : 67 #>   Confidence level: 95% #>  #>   lower_limit       : -3.175372 #>   contrast          : 0.5710176 #>   upper_limit       : 4.317407 #>   variance          : 3.653673 #>   current_total_n   : 65 #>   current_total_cost: 1499 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE (sampling has ended: the budget is exhausted) #>  #>   Note: Sampling has ended because the budget cannot pay for another #>         observation: 1 of 1500 is left, and one more observation from a #>         group still below its criterion (groups 2 and 3) costs at least #>         10. attr(out, "n_per_group") #> [1] 28 13 24

code: # The worked example of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, pp. 637-638): the # number of age appropriate books in the homes of third graders. A home # visit costs 75 dollars and A = 1000 / 0.05^2. books <- c(36, 53, 19, 11, 10, 24, 14, 65, 18, 48, 25, 35, 13, 18, 3, 41,            5, 3, 44, 26, 13, 39, 2, 3, 26, 22, 8, 15, 12, 22, 5, 21, 23,            40, 18) m <- seq_mr_cv_pilot(A = 400000, c = 75) m #> [1] 18  # After the pilot sample the rule is not met, so sampling continues. seq_mr_cv(books[1:m], A = 400000, c = 75) #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation)) #>  #>   Current n       : 18 #>   Criterion n     : 36 #>  #>   cv                : 0.7391157 #>   risk              : 5354.513 #>   xi_squared        : 0.1802031 #>   optimal_n         : 36 #>   current_n         : 18 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # With all 35 observations the default (corrected) variance asks for one # more; the article's own variance reproduces its printed result (risk # 4891.284, stop at 35). seq_mr_cv(books, A = 400000, c = 75) #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation)) #>  #>   Current n       : 35 #>   Criterion n     : 36 #>  #>   cv                : 0.7013904 #>   risk              : 4977.259 #>   xi_squared        : 0.2058226 #>   optimal_n         : 36 #>   current_n         : 35 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE seq_mr_cv(books, A = 400000, c = 75, variance = "published") #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation)) #>  #>   Current n       : 35 #>   Criterion n     : 35 #>  #>   cv                : 0.7013904 #>   risk              : 4891.284 #>   xi_squared        : 0.1982998 #>   optimal_n         : 35 #>   current_n         : 35 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE #>  #>   Note: The variance estimate is Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and #>         Kelley (2016), as requested with variance = "published". It #>         agrees with the default estimator for normal data and can #>         differ otherwise; see ?seq_mr_cv.

code: # Mean order value for an online retailer, in dollars. An error of one # dollar (squared) is worth 400 dollars and auditing one more order # costs 0.25 dollars. Times are simulated here with a mean of 6 # minutes, so the best sample size is sqrt(100 / 0.04) * 6 = 300. set.seed(113) m <- seq_mr_exp_mean_pilot(A = 100, c = 0.04) minutes <- rexp(m, rate = 1 / 6) out <- seq_mr_exp_mean(minutes, A = 100, c = 0.04) out #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (exponential mean)) #>  #>   Current n       : 8 #>   Criterion n     : 233 #>  #>   mean              : 4.642232 #>   risk              : 269.699 #>   optimal_n         : 233 #>   current_n         : 8 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # Add one ticket at a time until the stopping rule is met. while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   minutes <- c(minutes, rexp(1, rate = 1 / 6))   out <- seq_mr_exp_mean(minutes, A = 100, c = 0.04) } out #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (exponential mean)) #>  #>   Current n       : 295 #>   Criterion n     : 295 #>  #>   mean              : 5.897602 #>   risk              : 23.59041 #>   optimal_n         : 295 #>   current_n         : 295 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

code: # Shortest possible delivery time for an online retailer, in days. An # error of one day is valued at 500 dollars and tracking one more order # costs 0.25 dollars. Times are simulated here as a minimum of 2 days # plus an exponential delay averaging 1.5 days, so the best sample size # is sqrt(500 * 1.5 / 0.25), about 55. set.seed(113) m <- seq_mr_nexp_mean_pilot(A = 500, c = 0.25, k = 1, t = 1) days <- 2 + rexp(m, rate = 1 / 1.5) out <- seq_mr_nexp_mean(days, A = 500, c = 0.25, k = 1, t = 1) out #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (negative exponential location)) #>  #>   Current n       : 7 #>   Criterion n     : 50 #>  #>   location          : 2.15913 #>   risk              : 90.03639 #>   optimal_n         : 50 #>   current_n         : 7 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # Add one order at a time until the stopping rule is met. while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   days <- c(days, 2 + rexp(1, rate = 1 / 1.5))   out <- seq_mr_nexp_mean(days, A = 500, c = 0.25, k = 1, t = 1) } out #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (negative exponential location)) #>  #>   Current n       : 53 #>   Criterion n     : 53 #>  #>   location          : 2.001436 #>   risk              : 26.17606 #>   optimal_n         : 53 #>   current_n         : 53 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

code: # A school district wants its mean test score. An error of one point # (squared) is valued at 2,500 dollars and testing one more student # costs 4 dollars. Scores are simulated here with a standard deviation # of 12, so the best sample size is sqrt(2500 / 4) * 12 = 300. set.seed(113) m <- seq_mr_norm_mean_pilot(A = 2500, c = 4) scores <- rnorm(m, mean = 70, sd = 12) out <- seq_mr_norm_mean(scores, A = 2500, c = 4) out #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (normal mean)) #>  #>   Current n       : 5 #>   Criterion n     : 316 #>  #>   mean              : 70.97121 #>   risk              : 79636.06 #>   optimal_n         : 316 #>   current_n         : 5 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # Add one student at a time until the stopping rule is met. while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {   scores <- c(scores, rnorm(1, mean = 70, sd = 12))   out <- seq_mr_norm_mean(scores, A = 2500, c = 4) } out #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (normal mean)) #>  #>   Current n       : 299 #>   Criterion n     : 299 #>  #>   mean              : 69.45986 #>   risk              : 2386.488 #>   optimal_n         : 299 #>   current_n         : 299 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

code: # The pilot data of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017, p. 105): reading # scores of children with high and low exposure to same language # subtitling. Assessing one child costs 2.40 dollars; A = 2500 / 0.5^2. high_sls <- c(11, 7, 22, 13, 6, 9, 11, 16, 12, 17, 14, 8, 16) low_sls  <- c(3, 6, 10, 8, 14, 5, 12, 10, 6, 8, 13, 5, 9) seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = 10000, c = 2.40) #> [1] 13 seq_mr_smd(high_sls, low_sls, A = 10000, c = 2.40) #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (standardized mean difference)) #>  #>   Current n       : 26 #>   Criterion n     : 164 #>  #>   smd               : 1.021484 #>   risk              : 1801.521 #>   mean_1            : 12.46154 #>   mean_2            : 8.384615 #>   optimal_n1        : 82 #>   optimal_n2        : 82 #>   current_n1        : 13 #>   current_n2        : 13 #>   next_n1           : 14 #>   next_n2           : 14 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: FALSE  # Two costs: a visit to a child in the second group costs twice as much. # While the rule is not met, bring each group up to the size in its # next_n row and check again. The rows follow the article's sampling # order whichever group is the costlier one, so the loop also runs as # written with cost <- c(6, 3). set.seed(113) A <- 2000 cost <- c(3, 6)                  # group 1, group 2 true_mean <- c(0.5, 0) m <- seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = A, c = cost) y <- list(rnorm(m[["group_1"]], mean = true_mean[1]),           rnorm(m[["group_2"]], mean = true_mean[2])) check <- seq_mr_smd(y[[1]], y[[2]], A = A, c = cost) while (!attr(check, "is_satisfied")) {   next_n <- check$value[check$term %in% c("next_n1", "next_n2")]   for (j in 1:2) {     y[[j]] <- c(y[[j]],                 rnorm(next_n[j] - length(y[[j]]), mean = true_mean[j]))   }   check <- seq_mr_smd(y[[1]], y[[2]], A = A, c = cost) } check #> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (standardized mean difference)) #>  #>   Current n       : 51 #>   Criterion n     : 51 #>  #>   smd               : 0.2240416 #>   risk              : 378.5003 #>   mean_1            : 0.5786443 #>   mean_2            : 0.3443293 #>   optimal_n1        : 31 #>   optimal_n2        : 20 #>   current_n1        : 31 #>   current_n2        : 20 #>   next_n1           : 31 #>   next_n2           : 20 #>  #>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

The confidence level is #> asymptotic; meeting the width target does not establish nominal #> coverage at this sample size. #>  #> Reference #> Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018).
